notes: \cpara{Opens with a childhood memory, marked ``if I recall correctly'': a synagogue's annual appeal, where members called out their pledges from their seats. The post returns to it at the end.}
\cpara{Introduces the author's own appeal, made online to an audience from the ``atheist\slash{}libertarian\slash{}technophile'' cluster.}

\cfact{The link is to a LessWrong wiki page on a rule of the site's first months: no discussion of the Singularity or artificial general intelligence until the end of April 2009. The page says the ``Institute that Must Not be Named'' is the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, then called the Singularity Institute.}
\cpara{Says the appeal was written with care and sent to the mailing lists of the likely supporters.}
\cpara{The central anecdote, told from memory by the person who ran the appeal: critics posted their reasons for not giving, and suggested other sources of money.}

\cpara{Raises the obvious objection, that the criticisms might have been right, and defers it. The answer comes in the last two paragraphs: objections belong at another time, or should be voiced alongside support.}
\cpara{Donations were arriving, some with notes of thanks; the post quotes one.}
\cpara{The contrast the post turns on: no donor said so on the lists.}
\cpara{Draws the consequence: each donor saw only the objections.}
\cpara{Restates the scene in the synagogue's terms.}

\cpara{Introduces the comparison with the Raelians. Many Raelians call their creed an ``atheistic religion'' (Wikipedia, ``Raëlism,'' citing scholars of religion). So the contrast is not between believers and unbelievers, which fits the post's later diagnosis, about group culture.}
\cfact{The figures appear to be the movement's own. Wikipedia says it ``claims tens of thousands of members.'' I could not reach the interview the post links, so the 40,000 is unchecked.}
\cpara{Rejects imitating the cult, on ethical grounds and because, the post suggests with ``may,'' famous cults are the survivors of many that failed.}
\cpara{Warns against resenting a group one thinks inferior.}
\cpara{Turns the comparison into a question for the post's own readers.}
\cpara{Describes the first force that binds such groups: members who see only agreement grow more confident.}
\cpara{Names it pluralistic ignorance; the link is to ``On Expressing Your Concerns'' (2007).}
\cpara{The second force: doubters leave, and those who remain agree more.}
\cpara{Names it; the link is to ``Evaporative Cooling of Group Beliefs'' (2007).}

\cpara{The third force: praise feeds on itself. The preservative finding is from Finucane and colleagues, reported in ``The Affect Heuristic''; ``The Halo Effect'' treats the halo effect as the affect heuristic's form in social psychology.}
\cpara{Names it; the link is to ``Affective Death Spirals'' (2007).}
\cpara{Sums up the three forces.}

\cpara{States, in order to reject it, the view that the ``Light Side'' must always lose to the better coordinated ``Dark.'' The absolutes (``always,'' ``never,'' ``inevitably'') belong to the view under attack; the next paragraphs answer it.}
\cpara{Says that one's reaction to that prospect shows one's attitude to rationality.}
\cpara{No writer is named, and the motive given for them is a guess (``I suppose they're trying to signal their cynical sophistication or something'').}
\cpara{The author's answer: a true rationalist ought to be effective in the real world.}
\cpara{Applies it: the better coordinated side should not be the one that reasons worse.}
\cpara{Asks whether unreason must not have its disadvantages.}
\cpara{Leaves the reader to finish the syllogism: groups that cannot coordinate are not yet rational.}
\cpara{Introduces the post's diagnosis: half a rationalist is dangerous.}
\cpara{Restates the warning of ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People'' (2007), which the paragraph links, and marks its claim about smart people with ``I suspect.''}
\cpara{Extends the point to groups: teaching only individual rationality leaves a group unable to act together.}

\cpara{Names the first of two forces that keep the crowd from coordinating, the ``culture of objections''; the second comes later. The next day's post, ``Tolerate Tolerance,'' is also about working together: ``if we want to get anything done together.''}
\cpara{Begins an imagined contrast. The first version is the ordinary question line, full of objections.}
\cpara{The second version: a question line of praise. The evidence offered is the reader's imagined discomfort, and the next paragraphs play it for comedy.}
\cpara{The punch line: the listener flees in terror.}
\cpara{Draws the lesson: tolerating disagreement but not agreement is also irrational.}
\cpara{Restates it with the flying-saucer cult, and points to ``Reversed Stupidity Is Not Intelligence'' (2007).}
\cpara{Sets up a second example: an army in which only officers know strategy, against one in which everyone does.}
\cpara{Asks whether the ignorant, obedient army should win.}
\cpara{Answers that a group that truly understood military theory would know an uncoordinated mob loses.}

\cpara{States the principle: more knowledge should not make you do worse. For one decision maker this is the standard result that information cannot have negative value, because the decision maker ``can always ignore the additional information'' (Wikipedia, ``Value of information''). The post applies it to an army.}
\cpara{The ``lovely experiment'' is Taber and Lodge (2006), the one study in ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People.'' The notes on that post describe its samples and its predictions.}
\cpara{Sums up, with ``would seem,'' and concedes that the group's smaller efforts may be better aimed.}
\cpara{The remedy: train agreement as well as dissent, conformity as well as nonconformity.}
\cpara{Anticipates the reader's horror at practising agreement, and asks why practising disagreement is acceptable.}
\cpara{Offers, with ``Perhaps,'' the culture of objections as the reason the crowd stays marginalized. The description of the community is the author's own observation.}

\cfact{For information, two cases from the year before the post. Supporters of Ron Paul, the Libertarian Party's 1988 presidential nominee, organized a one-day online drive on 5 November 2007 that raised over \$4.2 million. In Britain an atheist bus-advertising drive gathered 877 of the 4,679 pledges it needed by July 2008; relaunched in October with Richard Dawkins matching gifts, it raised over \pounds100,000 in four days against a target of \pounds5,500. Such groups have coordinated giving at times, and have also failed to.}
\cpara{The second force, ``being ashamed of strong feelings.'' It restates ``Feeling Rational'' (2007), which the paragraph links.}
\cpara{Tests the reader's discomfort with a speaker willing to die for a cause.}
\cpara{Says that probability theory and decision theory do not forbid caring. Decision theory takes what an agent values as given, so the point is correct.}

\cpara{The quoted line is P.~C. Hodgell's; the author credits it to Hodgell in ``Twelve Virtues of Rationality'' and ``Feeling Rational.'' The paragraph restates the rule of ``Feeling Rational'': feel the emotions that fit the facts.}
\cpara{Pairs Hodgell's line with the author's own, from ``Feeling Rational'': ``That which the truth nourishes should thrive.''}
\cpara{Grants that science papers may need to avoid emotional language, but not everywhere else.}
\cpara{Restates the double rule: turn away from bad causes, and praise good ones.}

\cpara{Returns to the synagogue as the model: plain public pledges encourage others. The claim, offered with ``probably,'' has experimental support. In a field experiment on charitable giving, Shang and Croson (2009) found that telling donors what someone else had given raised the gifts of new members, though not of renewing ones; in the best condition, ``social information increases contributions by 12\% (\$13).''}
\cpara{Answers the objection deferred at the start: supporting and opposing opinions should both be voiced. Ends by calling a wall of objections the ``mirror image'' of what ``Dark Side groups'' do.}
